one_liner: Rust wc alternative with table/JSON output; beats GNU wc on chars and words in a UTF-8 locale, loses on bytes.
what_it_does: wz counts lines, words, characters, bytes and the longest line for one or more files, stdin, or a list of paths read from stdin (--from-stdin). It prints one row per file plus a Total row, as a box-drawn table (rounded by default; ascii, psql, markdown and extended styles) or as JSON with --output json. It is not a drop-in wc: the flags differ (-c is characters, -b is bytes) and so does the output format.
how_it_is_fast: Each enabled counter is a trait object chained in a small linked list ('Sheath') allocated in a bumpalo arena, and every counter sees the same read buffer of about 10 KB. Lines use bytecount::count and characters use bytecount::num_chars, which counts bytes that are not UTF-8 continuation bytes with runtime-dispatched SSE2/AVX2. Words are a scalar fold over ASCII-whitespace transitions, and bytes just add up the buffer lengths. With more than one file, rayon counts files in parallel. Most of the measured gain comes from skipping GNU wc's per-character multibyte decoding and from that parallelism, not from a faster algorithm with the same semantics.
when_to_use: Counting many files at once when you want a per-file table or a JSON summary with totals instead of wc's columns.
Character counts of valid UTF-8 text, where GNU wc -m in a UTF-8 locale decodes every character and is about 10x slower on the author's runner.
Word counts of text whose whitespace is ASCII (English or European prose, source code, logs).
Multi-core machines with many files: rayon spreads files across cores (there is no parallelism inside a single file).
Old Mac files with CR-only line breaks (-n cr).
when_not_to_use: Scripts that parse wc output or rely on wc's flags and exit status.
Byte counts alone: wz reads every byte, while GNU wc -c answers from the file size, and BENCH.md shows wz 2.4x slower.
Line length by display width (-L), or text with Unicode spaces such as U+3000 ideographic space: the answers differ from GNU wc (see gotchas).
Large single files: nothing larger than the 2.4 MB world192.txt was measured, reads go through a buffer of about 10 KB, and one file uses one thread.
UTF-16 input (the README lists it as 'coming later'; the encoding option offers only UTF8), or anything needing upkeep: no author changes since 1.0.3 in November 2022.

integration.form: crate (binary; cargo install wz); the counters are also published as the no_std crate wz-utf8
integration.dependencies: rayon, bumpalo, bytecount (runtime-dispatch-simd), memchr, clap 4, tabled, terminal_size, serde, serde_json
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 2021 edition; Cargo workspace dependency inheritance needs Cargo 1.64 or later; no rust-version declared, and Cargo.lock was removed from the repo on 2023-01-01
integration.platforms: any Rust target; SIMD only through bytecount's runtime dispatch on x86/x86-64 (SSE2, AVX2), with scalar fallbacks elsewhere; performance on non-x86-64 is unvalidated (issue #11, open)
integration.thread_safety: not applicable (CLI); files are counted in parallel on rayon's global pool
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: same quantities as wc, but -c means characters (wc -m) and -b means bytes (wc -c), output is a table or JSON with a Total row, -L counts characters rather than display columns, and the exit status is 0 even when a file cannot be opened

gotchas: Errors do not fail the run. A missing or unreadable file becomes an 'error' row in the table or JSON, and main still returns Ok, so the exit status is 0. The default table is truncated with '...' to the terminal width (80 columns when piped), so use --output json in scripts.

-L counts UTF-8 characters per line, not display columns. wz's own test expects "One\ntwo\t\nanother" to give 7, counting the tab as one character, whereas GNU wc -L expands tabs to 8-column stops and counts wide characters as two. Correction to the record: BENCH.md publishes no -L table because at its commit (585793b, 2022-09-09) the -L flag did not exist yet and the max-length line in bench/bench.sh was commented out, not because the result went unpublished.

Words split only on ASCII whitespace (0x20, 0x09, 0x0A-0x0D), and characters count non-continuation bytes without validating UTF-8 (its own test expects the invalid bytes \xF1\xF3 to count as 2 characters). The 10.5x chars and 2.7x words wins therefore compare this byte-level shortcut against GNU wc's locale-aware multibyte decoding, and counts can differ on Unicode spaces or invalid UTF-8. The runner's locale was not recorded; a user report says the ubuntu-20.04 runner image is C.UTF-8, and under LC_ALL=C GNU wc would not decode at all.

The comparison mixes parallel and serial work: wz runs rayon over the 11 files (33 in the high-load case) on 2 vCPUs, while GNU wc is single-threaded. Every run takes 0.8-60 ms on about 3.2 MB of input, so process start-up is a large share of each timing.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick wz over cw when you want table or JSON output across many files and fast UTF-8 character counts. cw was measured on a 341 MB file against GNU wc 8.30 and FreeBSD wc, with gains on lines and default counts, so it is the better-evidenced choice for big single files. hwc and the Haskell and APL wc experiments are demonstrations rather than maintained tools.
verified_claims_summary: Only the author's single hyperfine run backs the claim (BENCH.md, committed 2022-09-09), on a 2-vCPU GitHub Actions runner (Intel Xeon Platinum 8272CL) over 11 test files of about 3.2 MB, against the runner's GNU wc. The rustc version, wc version and locale were not recorded; ubuntu-latest was then probably Ubuntu 20.04, an inference. wz took 1.9 vs 19.8 ms for chars, 7.5 vs 20.5 ms for words, 7.3 vs 21.4 ms in default mode, 14.9 vs 58.2 ms on 33 files and 1.8 vs 2.2 ms for lines, and lost bytes at 1.9 vs 0.8 ms. The counter code for these modes is unchanged from that commit to HEAD apart from doc comments.
status_note: Abandoned: the last author change was release 1.0.3 on 2022-11-04, followed only by dependabot merges up to 2023-08-01, and there are no GitHub release binaries. It is MIT-licensed, small and readable, and installable from crates.io (wz 1.0.3, about 10,900 downloads, 4 stars).
